title: The Spring That Deflected 25.6 mm Under 500 N
featured_title: THE SPRING THAT DEFLECTED 25.6 MM UNDER 500 N

presentation.challenge: The spring force was 500 N, but the deflection depended strongly on wire diameter, coil diameter, and active coils.

practice.primary_question: How do wire diameter, mean coil diameter, active coils, and shear modulus determine helical spring stiffness?
practice.typical_exam_trap: Using F=kx without first calculating the spring rate from the spring geometry.

case_dna.target_misconception: A compression spring's stiffness can be inferred from force alone without using its geometry and material properties.
case_dna.why_plausible: Hooke's law F=kx is simple, so the challenge of determining k can be overlooked.
case_dna.contradicting_evidence: For d=8 mm, D=64 mm, N=8, and G=80 GPa, k=d⁴G/(8D³N)≈19.53 N/mm. Under 500 N, x=F/k≈25.6 mm.
case_dna.corrected_model: Calculate helical spring rate from geometry and shear modulus, then use F=kx.

problem_statement: A helical compression spring has wire diameter 8 mm, mean coil diameter 64 mm, 8 active coils, and shear modulus G=80 GPa. It carries a 500 N load. A technician uses an arbitrary 50 N/mm stiffness. Determine the actual spring rate and deflection.

gates.label: Incident
gates.heading: The load was known. The spring rate had to come from geometry.
gates.prompt: Which dimensions control the spring rate?

options.label: Use k=d⁴G/(8D³N), then x=F/k
options.reason: This is the standard linear helical compression-spring rate model.

options.label: Use force alone to infer stiffness
options.reason: Spring stiffness depends on material and geometry.

options.label: Assume spring rate is proportional to mean coil diameter D
options.reason: Spring rate varies inversely with D³.

gates.label: Predict
gates.heading: Predict spring deflection
gates.prompt: Approximately how many millimeters does the spring deflect under 500 N?

gates.label: Gap
gates.heading: Prove the spring rate
gates.prompt: Use k=d⁴G/(8D³N). Enter k in N/mm.

cards.text: Mean coil diameter enters as D³ in the denominator.
k≈19.53 N/mm, so x≈25.6 mm at 500 N.

gates.heading: Correct the spring calculation
report: C3. Any convenient stiffness can be inserted into F=kx without checking geometry.

claims.label: C3
claims.reason: The spring rate must be calculated from geometry and material properties.

evidence_choices.label: k=d⁴G/(8D³N)≈19.53 N/mm
evidence_choices.reason: This is the correct spring-rate calculation.

gates.heading: Increase spring stiffness

Increase mean coil diameter

gates.prompt: If the number of active coils doubles while everything else stays fixed, what happens to k?

options.label: It doubles
options.reason: More active coils make the spring more compliant.

seo.seo_title: Helical Spring Rate: Why 500 N Causes 25.6 mm Deflection | FE E-058
seo.meta_description: Solve FE Mechanical Case E-058: an 8 mm wire, 64 mm mean-diameter spring with 8 active coils has k≈19.53 N/mm and deflects 25.6 mm at 500 N.
seo.excerpt: Hooke's law is only useful after the spring rate is determined from material and coil geometry.
seo.direct_answer: For a helical compression spring, k=d⁴G/(8D³N). With d=8 mm, D=64 mm, N=8, and G=80 GPa, k≈19.53 N/mm. A 500 N load therefore causes about 25.6 mm deflection.

faqs.q: What is the helical compression spring rate formula?
faqs.a: k=d⁴G/(8D³N) for the idealized linear model.

faqs.q: What happens if active coil count increases?
